589.title: The sage
589.hook: the sage has no house to guard and no friendships built on fear
589.howItsDone: Buddhists call the Buddha Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas, and the ideal of the quiet, unattached sage runs through the poems of the Sutta Nipata.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kaya, the body seen plainly, and your line, as it is. Today, the last poem of the first chapter, and an old word for a wise person.

Count the things you have to keep an eye on. Passwords. The car's next service. The plant that's dying. Subscriptions you forgot. Friends who'd be upset if you didn't reply by tonight. None of it is bad. But each one is a small hook, and some days a life is mostly hooks. The Buddha's India had a word for a person who'd taken most of the hooks out. Not a priest, not a scholar. Someone quiet, wise, unattached, often wandering. The twelfth poem of the Sutta Nipata is about that person.
screen: `PASSWORDS, PLANTS, REPLIES.` → `SOME DAYS IT'S MOSTLY HOOKS.` → `A WORD FOR SOMEONE WITHOUT THEM.`

segments.voice: Muni means sage, a silent, wise one. The Buddha himself is called Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakya people. The Muni Sutta opens with a strong line. From intimacy, fear is born. From a home, dust arises. To be without a home and without that kind of clinging: that's the sage's way of seeing. It sounds harsh until you hear the word underneath. Santhava, the intimacy here, means acquaintance, familiarity, and the commentary reads it as the binding kind, closeness held by craving. Closeness like that comes with fear of losing it. The sage isn't cold; it's the clinging the poem warns against. Then come pictures. The sage stands firm, like a post at a river's bathing place, while other people talk in extremes around it, praise and blame splashing on every side. The sage lives on what is given, and doesn't flatter the giver or complain about the gift. At the very end comes a frank image: a blue-necked peacock never matches the speed of a swan in flight, and in the same way, the poem says, a householder doesn't match a sage meditating alone in the forest. That's the poem's view of the wandering life. Other Buddhist texts honor lay life and remember lay followers who were wise teachers. One more twist, from the Dhammapada: nobody becomes a muni just by keeping silent. A fool can be quiet. The sage is the one who weighs things well and chooses the good.

Then picture the post at the river, praise and blame splashing around it, and feel yourself that steady for a few breaths.
Muni. A sage, a silent wise one: no house to guard, no friendships built on fear, steady as a post while praise and blame splash by. Today's word.
Your line: stand like the post. Praise and blame splash by; the post stays. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

590.title: The jewel discourse
590.hook: a city in crisis, and a verse chanted along its walls through the night
590.howItsDone: The Ratana Sutta is one of the paritta, or protective texts, of Theravada Buddhism; monks chant it at blessings, for the sick, and in times of public crisis, often over a bowl of water that is then sprinkled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: muni, the sage, and your line, stand like the post. Today a new chapter of the Sutta Nipata begins, in a city in trouble.

Vesali was a rich city, run by a council of nobles called the Licchavis. And then, the story goes, everything went wrong at once. The rains failed. Crops died. People starved, and sickness spread through the streets, and the city was full of dread. The council sent messengers south to Rajagaha to ask the Buddha to come. He came. And the tradition says that the moment he set foot in their territory, the sky opened and it poured. Then he gave Ananda a set of verses to carry through the city.
screen: `VESALI: FAMINE AND SICKNESS.` → `MESSENGERS TO RAJAGAHA.` → `THE SKY OPENS.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Ratana Sutta, the discourse on the jewel. The story around it comes from the commentary: Ananda walked along the city walls all night, chanting the verses and sprinkling water from the Buddha's bowl, and the city recovered. The poem itself starts by speaking to every being gathered there, visible or not: may all of you be happy, and listen. Show kindness to the humans who bring you offerings day and night, and protect them. Then come the verses that give it its name. Whatever treasure there is in this world or any other, nothing equals the one who has fully awakened. Then a line that ends verse after verse, like a bell. In Pali: etena saccena suvatthi hotu. By this truth, may there be well-being. It's called an act of truth. Behind it is an old Indian idea: that stating something deeply true, solemnly, has power. So the poem states truths: the Buddha is a jewel, the teaching is a jewel, the community of noble disciples is a jewel. And on each truth, it rests a wish for safety. One verse near the end holds a quiet image. The old is used up, nothing new arises; the wise go out, the poem says, like this lamp. Picture Ananda saying that at night, perhaps holding a flame. Theravada monks still chant this poem when a home is blessed and when someone is sick.

Ratana, jewel. The Ratana Sutta: truths about the Buddha, the teaching and the community, each one ending with a wish for well-being, chanted in times of fear. Today's word.
Your line: the jewel. A true thing, said gently for someone else's safety. Until tomorrow.

591.title: The smell of deeds
591.hook: a strict ascetic asks a buddha about the smell of raw flesh, and gets a list of deeds
591.howItsDone: Theravada monastics accept the food lay people offer, including meat not killed for them, while Mahayana monasteries in China, Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam keep a vegetarian diet, as do some lay Buddhists.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ratana, the jewel discourse, and your line, the jewel. Today, an argument about dinner.

Some people have strong views about what's on your plate. Sometimes it's you. And food rules are serious things: they shape families, holidays, whole communities. The second poem of the second chapter is an argument about food, set long before the Buddha we know. It's told about Kassapa, a buddha the tradition says lived in an earlier age. An ascetic named Tissa, who eats only wild grain, beans, leaves and fruit, sees him accept a meal with meat in it. And Tissa challenges him.
screen: `WHAT'S ON YOUR PLATE?` → `A BUDDHA OF AN EARLIER AGE.` → `AN ASCETIC'S CHALLENGE.`

segments.voice: Tissa's word is amagandha. Ama means raw, gandha means smell. The smell of raw flesh: in his world, a word for what is impure, rotten. The good ones, he says, live on what grows wild, honestly gathered. But you eat fine dishes cooked by others, rice with the meat of birds, and still you say the rotten smell doesn't touch you. So what do you mean by it? Kassapa's answer is a list, and the list is the point. Killing, beating, cutting, tying up. Stealing. Lying. Cheating, fraud, empty learning. Going after another's partner. People who are harsh, cruel, backbiting, betraying friends, heartless, stingy. Anger, pride, stubbornness, hypocrisy, envy, boasting, arrogance. This, he says, is the rotten smell, not the eating of meat. Fasting, going naked, shaving the head, offerings and rites, none of them cleans a person who hasn't let go of doubt. The rot is in deeds. The poem says the teacher explained it again and again, until Tissa understood, bowed, and asked to join. Tradition says the Buddha we know later retold the whole exchange. A plain word about Buddhists and food today, because traditions differ. Theravada monks and nuns eat what is offered, including meat, unless they saw, heard or suspect the animal was killed for them. Mahayana monasteries in China, Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam keep a vegetarian diet, drawing on later scriptures. Both read this poem. And on its own point, the poem is plain: the smell it names is cruelty and lying.
screen: `AMAGANDHA: THE SMELL OF RAW FLESH` · `KILLING, LYING, CHEATING, CRUELTY` · `THE ROT IS IN DEEDS` · `BUDDHISTS TODAY EAT DIFFERENTLY` · then, large: `THE SMELL OF DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day or two for a moment that, if deeds had a smell, would smell a little off, a sharp word, a small lie, a bit of gossip. Amagandha, the smell of raw flesh. Kassapa's answer to Tissa: the real rot isn't in the food, it's in cruelty, lies and pride. Today's word.
Your line: open the window. The rot was never on the plate. Day five hundred ninety-one, done.

592.title: A real friend
592.hook: a friend isn't the one who says 'I'm your friend'; it's the one who stands by you
592.carry: a child asleep on a parent's chest
592.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers read the Hiri Sutta alongside the advice to Sigala on true and false friends, as practical guidance for lay friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: amagandha, the smell of deeds, and your line, open the window. Today, a short poem about friendship that fits on an index card.

You're moving apartments. Forty boxes, a couch, a Saturday in August. In the group chat, a dozen people said, of course, anything you need! At eight in the morning, two of them show up. Those two are the ones the day belongs to. A few weeks ago, the advice to Sigala gave a way to tell true friends from false ones. The third poem of this chapter is shorter and sharper: five verses about the gap between saying and doing.
screen: `FORTY BOXES AND A COUCH.` → `A DOZEN SAID YES. TWO CAME.` → `SAYING AND DOING.`

segments.voice: The poem is called the Hiri Sutta, after the word it begins with: hiri, a sense of shame, a conscience. It starts with someone who has none, who says I'm your friend, but never takes on any task they could easily do. Know them, the poem says: they're not my friend. Then: someone who speaks pleasant words to friends but doesn't follow through. The wise see that person clearly: all talk, no doing. Then a surprise. It's also not a friend who is always on alert for a break, watching you for faults, keeping score. Friendship that's suspicious is its own kind of failure. And then the picture of the real thing. A real friend is the one you can rest on, the poem says, like a child asleep on a parent's chest. Someone others can't split you away from. Stay with that image. A child on a parent's chest doesn't check, doesn't wonder whether it's safe, doesn't earn its place. It just rests. That's what being a real friend makes possible for someone else. And it's built by deeds, not speeches: showing up, doing the task you could do, not keeping a list of the other person's mistakes. The poem's last verses turn inward, to the quiet joy of a good life and of the teaching. As if to say: the kind of person who can be that friend is someone at peace enough not to need the credit.
screen: `I'M YOUR FRIEND, BUT NO HELP` · `ALL TALK, NO DOING` · `NOT ALWAYS WATCHING FOR FAULTS` · `A CHILD ASLEEP ON A PARENT'S CHEST` · then, large: `A REAL FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who could use a friend to rest on right now, someone moving, grieving, overwhelmed or just quiet lately, and picture what would actually help: not let me know if you need anything, but one specific thing. Then let go of any score you've been keeping with them, and rest with the breath.
Mitta, friend. Not the one who says I'm your friend, but the one who does the task, doesn't keep score, and can be rested on like a parent's chest. Today's word.
Your line: a child asleep on a parent's chest. The kind of friend someone can rest on. That's day five hundred ninety-two.

593.title: The highest blessings
593.hook: the gods ask what truly brings good fortune; the first answer is about company
593.howItsDone: The Mangala Sutta is among the most widely chanted protective texts in Theravada Buddhism; it is recited at weddings, house blessings and new beginnings, and many children learn it by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mitta, the friend you can rest on, and your line, a child asleep on a parent's chest. Today begins a poem that stays for four days.
screen: `A CHILD ASLEEP ON A PARENT'S CHEST.`

segments.voice: Lucky socks on game day. Knocking on wood. Not walking under a ladder. A lucky number on the apartment door. Every culture has its signs of good fortune, and the Buddha's India had plenty. The commentary tells a story: people argued for years about what was truly auspicious. Was it something you see, like a bird or a pot of water? Something you hear, a good word on waking? Something you touch? The argument spread, the story says, all the way up to the gods. So one night a god came down to the Jeta Grove to ask the Buddha.
screen: `LUCKY SOCKS. KNOCK ON WOOD.` → `WHAT IS TRULY AUSPICIOUS?` → `A GOD COMES TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Mangala means blessing, good fortune, an auspicious sign. The poem is the Mangala Sutta, and it opens with the visitor's question: many gods and humans have thought about blessings, longing for well-being. Tell us the highest. Notice what the Buddha doesn't do. He doesn't say omens are silly. He just answers with a different kind of sign, one you can see in a life. Not keeping company with fools. Keeping company with the wise. Honoring those who deserve honor. That's the highest blessing, he says. That's the first verse. Your life starts with who you sit next to. Then the next verse: living in a good place, having done good in the past, setting yourself on the right course. Then: much learning, a skill or craft, being well trained, and speech that is well spoken. That's the highest blessing. The poem keeps going, verse after verse, and the tradition counts thirty-eight blessings in all. Each verse ends with the same line, which works like a stamp: this is the highest blessing. Here's what makes it different from lucky socks. An omen happens to you. These blessings are things you can do. Choose your company. Learn something well. Speak well. Fortune, in this poem, isn't waiting outside your door. It's built into how you live. Tomorrow, the poem comes home: to parents, family and work.

594.title: Blessings at home
594.hook: the blessings poem walks into the house: parents, family, and work that isn't chaos
594.howItsDone: The Mangala Sutta is among the protective chants recited at Theravada blessings, and Buddhist teachers draw on its family verses, with the teaching on repaying parents, when they speak about home life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mangala, the highest blessings, and your line, choose your company. Today the same poem comes in through the front door.

A grandmother's hands, shelling peas at a kitchen table. A dad checking the lock twice before bed. Somebody picking up a parent's prescription on the way home from a long shift. None of it gets posted. None of it looks like a spiritual life. And yet the Buddha, asked by a god what the highest blessings are, gets to this exact scene a few verses in. Before meditation, before the deep teachings, the poem stops at home.
screen: `SHELLING PEAS. CHECKING THE LOCK.` → `NOTHING ANYONE POSTS.` → `THE POEM STOPS AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Supporting your mother and father. Caring for your partner and your children. Work that is peaceful, not tangled and chaotic. That is the highest blessing. The text, from its time, says wife and children; some readers today hear it as whoever makes up your household. Notice the three. Looking up the generations, to parents. Looking across and down, to partner and children. And the work that feeds them all, done without turmoil. In the Buddha's teaching, caring for parents isn't a small duty. Elsewhere he says that even carrying your parents on your shoulders for a hundred years wouldn't repay them, though helping them toward goodness and wisdom does. Then the next verse widens the circle. Giving. Living by what is right. Helping your relatives. Actions no one could fault. That is the highest blessing. And the next. Keeping away from wrongdoing. Holding back from intoxicants. Being steady and careful in what is good. Listen to how ordinary this is. Pay the bills honestly. Call your aunt. Don't drink yourself into a mess. Take care of the people who took care of you. The poem doesn't say these lead to the blessings. It says they are the blessings. A tidy, peaceful home, a parent fed, a cousin helped: these are not the waiting room of the spiritual life. In this poem, they're inside it.

Matapitu upatthanam, supporting mother and father. In the Mangala Sutta: caring for partner and children, peaceful work, giving and helping relatives. Not steps toward the blessing: the blessing itself. Today's word.

595.title: Blessings of the heart
595.hook: respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, and being easy to correct
595.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice gratitude through daily chanting, offerings to monastics and teachers, and merit-dedication ceremonies for parents and ancestors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: blessings at home, and your line, a blessing. Today ends the week, and the poem turns inward.

Someone at work points out a mistake in your report. Not cruelly; it's just wrong. And there's a tiny moment, maybe half a second, before you answer. A lot rides on that half second. Do you bristle, explain, defend? Or do you say: oh, you're right, thanks? The Mangala Sutta has a word for the second answer, and it calls it one of the highest blessings. So far the poem has covered company, learning, home and work. Now it reaches the qualities inside a person.
screen: `A MISTAKE IN YOUR REPORT.` → `HALF A SECOND TO ANSWER.` → `THE POEM TURNS INWARD.`

segments.voice: The verse goes: respect and humility, contentment and gratitude, and hearing the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing. Then the next: patience, being easy to correct, seeing those who live a holy life, and talking about the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing. Look at gratitude. The Pali is kataññuta. Kata, what was done; ññu, knowing. Gratitude is knowing what has been done for you. Not a feeling you have to manufacture. A kind of seeing: someone made this meal, someone taught me to read, someone kept the lights on. The Buddha elsewhere says that grateful people, those who know what has been done for them, are rare in the world. And look at being easy to correct, sovacassata. Literally, being good to speak to. The person you can tell something to without a fight. It sits right next to patience, and it's the half-second answer from the report. These are blessings because they open a person. Contentment leaves room. Humility lets teaching in. Gratitude lets you see. Look back at the week. The sage with no fear-built ties. The jewel, chanted on a truth. The smell of deeds, not of food. A friend you can rest on. Then wise company, home, and now the heart. Again and again this week, the good thing turned out to be something a person does or is, not something that happens to them.
screen: `RESPECT, HUMILITY, CONTENTMENT` · `GRATITUDE: KNOWING WHAT WAS DONE` · `EASY TO CORRECT, PATIENT` · `A WEEK OF WHAT A PERSON DOES` · then, large: `GRATITUDE IS A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you, a chair, a cup, the clothes you're wearing, and trace what was done for it to be here: someone grew the cotton, someone sewed, someone drove the truck, someone stocked the shelf. Don't force a warm feeling; just know what was done, then let one person who did something for you come to mind, and know that too.
Kataññuta, gratitude. In the Mangala Sutta: respect, humility, contentment, patience and being easy to correct, the blessings that open a person. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude is a blessing. It starts with seeing what was done. That's day five hundred ninety-five.
